stock.story: Imagine your class bakes one giant birthday cake and cuts it into 100 slices. If you hold 1 slice, you own 1 hundredth of the cake. If the cake becomes famous and everyone wants a piece, your slice becomes precious.
stock.link: A company is the cake and a share is your slice. If the company does well, more people want slices, so the price of your slice goes up.

price_close.story: Think of the score at the end of a cricket match. Lots happens during the match, but the final score is the one everyone remembers and compares with yesterday's.
price_close.link: The closing price is the share's final price when the market shuts for the day. Green means it ended higher than yesterday, red means lower.

candlestick.story: Imagine drawing how high a kid jumped on a trampoline today. One little box tells you where they started, where they finished, and thin lines show the highest and lowest bounce.
candlestick.link: Each candle on the chart is one day of a share's price. Green means it ended higher than it began, red means lower, and the thin lines are the day's highest and lowest prices.

paper_trading.story: When you play Monopoly you buy streets with toy money. You can win or lose the whole game and nobody loses a single real rupee, so you learn how the game works.
paper_trading.link: Paper trading is Monopoly with real share prices. You practise buying and selling with pretend money, so you learn without risking anything.

portfolio.story: Think of your school bag. It holds your books, your lunch and your water bottle. Everything you carry is in one place, and you can look inside to see what you have.
portfolio.link: Your portfolio is the bag that holds everything you own: your cash and your shares. Looking inside tells you how much it is all worth.

buy_sell.story: At a school fair you swap a coupon for a samosa. Later, if someone wants your coupon, you can swap it back for money. If you paid less than you got back, you made a little profit.
buy_sell.link: Buying means swapping money for shares. Selling means swapping shares back for money. You gain if you sell for more than you paid.

profit_loss.story: You sell lemonade. You spent Rs 50 on lemons and sugar and collected Rs 80 from customers. You made Rs 30. If you only collected Rs 40, you lost Rs 10.
profit_loss.link: Profit is when you get back more than you put in, and loss is when you get back less. For shares, it only becomes real money when you sell.

moving_average.story: Your marks in 50 tests are jumpy: 90, 40, 85, 60. Your teacher says 'your average is 72', which tells how you are really doing without worrying about one bad day.
moving_average.link: A moving average does that for a share's price: it smooths out the daily jumps so you can see the real direction.

bollinger_bands.story: Picture a school corridor with painted lines on both sides. A kid walking normally stays between the lines. When the corridor is wide, kids run around. When it is narrow, everyone walks calmly.
bollinger_bands.link: The grey band on the chart is the corridor for the price. Wide means the price is bouncing a lot, narrow means it is calm.

trend.story: Imagine walking on a hill. Going up, you keep rising even if you pause for a breath. Going down, you keep sliding. On flat ground, you just go sideways.
trend.link: A trend is the direction a price is walking: uphill (uptrend), downhill (downtrend) or flat (sideways).

support_resistance.story: When you bounce a ball in a room, it hits the floor and goes back up, and it hits the ceiling and comes back down. The floor and the ceiling stop it.
support_resistance.link: Support is a price floor where the share keeps bouncing up. Resistance is a ceiling where it keeps getting pushed down.

rsi.story: Think of a runner sprinting in a race. After a super fast sprint they are out of breath and need to slow down. After a long rest they are fresh and ready to run again.
rsi.link: RSI is a number from 0 to 100 that shows how fast a price has been racing. Very high means it sprinted up and may need a rest. Very low means it fell hard and may bounce back.

overbought_oversold.story: When a new toy arrives, everybody rushes to buy it and the shop runs out. A few days later the rush is over and things go quiet again.
overbought_oversold.link: Overbought means everybody rushed to buy a share, so the price ran up very fast. Oversold means everybody rushed to sell. After the rush, prices often calm down.

macd.story: Two friends are walking. One walks fast, one walks slowly. When the fast one pulls ahead, the group is speeding up. When the fast one drops behind the slow one, the group is slowing down.
macd.link: MACD compares a quick average of the price with a slow average. Quick pulling ahead means the price is gaining speed. Falling behind means it is losing speed.

momentum.story: A ball rolling down a slope keeps rolling for a while even if nobody pushes it again.
momentum.link: Momentum means a price that has been rising strongly often keeps rising for a bit, and a price that has been falling often keeps falling.

volatility.story: A smooth road is calm to ride on. A rocky mountain track makes your bicycle bounce up and down a lot.
volatility.link: Volatility is how bumpy a share's ride is. A calm share is the smooth road. A very volatile share has big jumps up and down.

average_return.story: A plant grows a different amount each week. Over a year, you measure how tall it got and say 'it grew about 5 cm every month on average'.
average_return.link: Average yearly return is the same idea for money: how much a share grew each year on average.

max_drawdown.story: You build a tall tower of blocks and it wobbles. The biggest drop from its tallest moment to its lowest point is the scariest fall your tower had.
max_drawdown.link: Maximum drawdown is the biggest fall a share had from a high point to a low point. It shows the scariest moment someone holding it would have lived through.

var.story: Think of rainy days. In 20 days of school, maybe 1 day is so rainy that the ground is full of puddles. You know to expect at least that much rain on the worst day.
var.link: Value at Risk says how much a share could fall on a bad day, one day in 20. It helps you prepare for the rainy days.

risk_free_rate.story: Keeping your pocket money in a safe piggy bank at home earns nothing but also loses nothing. A bank locker that adds a little extra is safe too.
risk_free_rate.link: The safe return is what you can earn without any risk, like lending to the government. A risky share should promise more than that, or why take the risk?

sharpe_ratio.story: Two kids go to school. One takes a quick path full of puddles and dogs. The other takes a slightly slower, smooth path. Who got the better deal depends on how much they gained for how much trouble they went through.
sharpe_ratio.link: The Sharpe ratio tells how much extra reward a share gave for each bump in the ride. More reward for fewer bumps is better.

sortino_ratio.story: On a roller coaster, going up is the fun part and only the sudden drops scare you. A fair score would only count the drops as scary.
sortino_ratio.link: The Sortino ratio is like the Sharpe ratio, but it only counts the falls as risk, because rising prices don't hurt anyone.

calmar_ratio.story: You scored well on your tests this year, but you also had one terrible test that made you cry. A fair review compares how well you did overall with how bad your worst moment was.
calmar_ratio.link: The Calmar ratio compares how much a share grew each year with its worst fall. Big growth with small falls scores high.

treynor_ratio.story: If the whole class is on a bus and the bus goes faster, everybody gets there earlier. A smart check is how much extra you gained for riding along with the bus.
treynor_ratio.link: The Treynor ratio checks how much extra return a share gave for going along with the whole market's ups and downs.

nifty50.story: The class average tells you how the whole class did on a test using one number. Then you can see if you scored above or below it.
nifty50.link: The Nifty 50 is the class average for India's 50 biggest companies. If a share does better than the Nifty, it beat the class.

beta.story: On a pond, a big wave comes. A heavy boat rocks only a little, but a tiny paper boat bounces everywhere.
beta.link: Beta tells how much a share bounces when the whole market makes a wave. Beta above 1 is the paper boat, and below 1 is the heavy boat.

alpha.story: Everyone in class got easy questions, so most kids scored high. If you scored even higher than everyone expected, you did something special.
alpha.link: Alpha is the extra return a share gave beyond what was expected from the market. Positive alpha means it beat expectations.

information_ratio.story: One kid scores slightly higher than the class every single test. Another scores very high once and very low the next time. The first is steadier.
information_ratio.link: The information ratio shows whether a share beat the market steadily or just by luck.

correlation.story: Two best friends who always walk to school together are tightly linked. Two kids who live in different towns are not linked at all.
correlation.link: Correlation says how closely a share moves together with the market. 1 means walking together, 0 means unrelated, below 0 means going opposite ways.

monte_carlo.story: Imagine rolling a dice 2,000 times to guess how far a toy car might travel on a bumpy road. You do not know what will really happen, but you see all the places it could end up.
monte_carlo.link: A Monte Carlo simulation imagines 2,000 possible futures for a share, using how bumpy it has been. It shows where the price could go, not where it will go.

probability_range.story: Drop 100 marbles through a funnel. Most land near the middle and a few roll far away. The pile looks like a fan.
probability_range.link: The fan chart is that pile for share prices. The darker the colour, the more of the pretend futures landed there.

chance_higher.story: You flip a coin 100 times, but this coin is a little bent. If 42 flips land heads, that tells you how this bent coin behaves, not what the next flip will do.
chance_higher.link: The gauge shows how many of the pretend futures ended higher than today. It describes the simulation, not the real future.

backtest.story: Before a real cricket match, you replay last year's match in your head with a new plan to see if it would have won.
backtest.link: A backtest replays old share prices using a trading rule to see how the rule would have done. It is a rehearsal, not a promise.

buy_and_hold.story: You plant a mango tree and then leave it alone for years. You do not dig it up every week to check on it.
buy_and_hold.link: Buy and hold means buying a share and keeping it, whatever happens. Any trading rule has to beat this simple plan to be worth using.

ma_crossover_rule.story: You decide to carry an umbrella only when the weather forecast says rain is coming, and leave it at home otherwise.
ma_crossover_rule.link: This rule owns the share only when the quick average is above the slow one (things look good), and waits in cash otherwise.

diversification.story: If you carry all your eggs in one basket and drop it, every egg breaks. If you use three baskets, dropping one still leaves two safe.
diversification.link: Diversification means spreading your money across different companies, so one bad one does not ruin everything.

dividend.story: You own a hen that lays eggs. Every few weeks she gives you a few eggs just for owning her, even if you never sell her.
dividend.link: A dividend is a small payment a company gives its owners from its profits, just for owning the shares.

risk_return.story: Climbing a taller tree gives a better view, but the fall is also bigger. A low branch is safer but the view is not as good.
risk_return.link: In investing, a bigger chance of a big reward usually comes with a bigger chance of a loss.

trading_costs.story: Every time you swap stickers at school, the friend who helps you keeps one small sticker as a fee. Swap a hundred times and your collection shrinks.
trading_costs.link: Every buy or sell costs a small fee. Trade too often and the fees quietly eat your profit.

stop_loss.story: When you ride a bicycle down a hill, you promise yourself to press the brake before you reach the bottom so you do not crash.
stop_loss.link: A stop-loss is a promise to sell if the price falls to a chosen level, so one bad fall cannot hurt you too much.

compounding.story: You roll a small snowball down a snowy hill. It picks up more snow as it rolls, and the bigger it gets, the more snow it picks up.
compounding.link: Compounding means your money earns money, and then that extra money earns more. Growth speeds up over time.

options_futures.story: You tell the toy shop: 'Keep this toy for me and I will pay today's price next month.' You are booking it early at a price you agreed on.
options_futures.link: Futures and options are agreements to buy or sell something later at a price fixed today. They can go very right or very wrong.

past_performance.story: Winning a game of ludo yesterday does not mean you will win it tomorrow. The dice are different each time.
past_performance.link: A rule that worked on old prices might not work next time, because markets change.

valuation.story: A toy costs Rs 500 in one shop and Rs 5,000 in another. Even the best toy is a bad buy if the price is far too high.
valuation.link: Valuation asks whether a share's price is fair, too high or a bargain compared with what the company earns and owns.

pe_ratio.story: A lemonade stand makes Rs 10 a year and someone asks Rs 200 for it. You would be paying for 20 years of profit to get your money back.
pe_ratio.link: The P/E ratio says how many years of profit you pay for when you buy a share. A high number means the share is expensive.

fundamental_analysis.story: Before buying a pet, you check whether it is healthy, eats well and has no illness.
fundamental_analysis.link: Fundamental analysis checks how healthy a company really is: its sales, profits and debts.

technical_analysis.story: A detective follows footprints in the mud to guess where someone walked and where they may go next.
technical_analysis.link: Technical analysis studies price charts, the footprints of buyers and sellers, to understand what the crowd is doing.

fusion_analysis.story: To pick a player for your cricket team, you check two things: is the player skilled, and is the player in good form right now?
fusion_analysis.link: Fusion analysis uses both checks together: is the company healthy (fundamentals) and is its price actually rising (technicals)?

winners_circle.story: Imagine three hoops on the ground that overlap in the middle. Standing in all three at once is hard, so whoever stands in the middle is special.
winners_circle.link: The Winner's Circle has three hoops: price going up, healthy company, fair price. The best shares sit in all three.

market_cap.story: If one slice of cake costs Rs 10 and the cake has 100 slices, the whole cake is worth Rs 1,000.
market_cap.link: Market cap is the price of the whole company: one share's price times the number of shares.

mean_reversion.story: A rubber band stretched too far snaps back towards the middle.
mean_reversion.link: Mean reversion means a price stretched far from normal often snaps back towards its average.

trend_following.story: A surfer waits for a big wave, rides it as long as it lasts, and steps off when it ends.
trend_following.link: Trend following means joining a price that is moving up and leaving when the move ends, instead of guessing the top or bottom.

whipsaw.story: Your friend says 'go left!' and then immediately 'no, go right!', so you keep turning and get nowhere.
whipsaw.link: A whipsaw is a signal that flips right after you act on it, so you buy and sell again and again and lose a little each time.

overfitting.story: You memorise last year's exam answers perfectly. You would score full marks on that paper but fail a new one.
overfitting.link: Overfitting is making a trading rule fit old prices perfectly, so it fails on new prices.

sentiment.story: When the whole class is excited about a school trip, everyone is smiling and the mood is high. When a test is announced, the mood drops.
sentiment.link: Sentiment is the market's mood. Happy moods push prices up (bull market) and scared moods push them down (bear market).

liquidity.story: A popular toy sells in seconds. A strange one-of-a-kind toy may sit in the shop for months because few people want it.
liquidity.link: Liquidity means how easily you can swap a share for money. Popular shares sell quickly, unpopular ones can be hard to sell.

hedging.story: You carry an umbrella even on a sunny day. You hope it will not rain, but if it does, you stay dry.
hedging.link: Hedging means making a small extra bet that protects you if your main investment falls.

stock_split.story: You cut one pizza into twice as many slices. You now have more slices, but each is smaller, so the total pizza is the same.
stock_split.link: In a stock split you get more shares at a lower price each, and your total value stays the same.

index_fund.story: Instead of choosing one fruit at the market, you buy a mixed basket that has a little of every fruit.
index_fund.link: An index fund holds a little of every company in a big group, like the Nifty 50, so you do not have to pick just one.

drift.story: A boat with no engine slowly floats in the direction the river is flowing.
drift.link: Drift is the direction a price has been slowly leaning on average. The simulation uses the past year's drift.
